one_liner: Java embedded key-value store for point lookups: append-only logs plus an off-heap hash index. Beats RocksDB on random writes and reads in IO-bound tests.
what_it_does: HaloDB is an embedded, persistent key-value store for the JVM. Yahoo built it to replace Kyoto Cabinet under a write-heavy ad-platform database that had 8-byte keys, large values, one writer thread and a working set far bigger than RAM. The API is small and not RocksDB-compatible: byte[] put/get/delete, an unordered full iterator and key iterator, snapshot, stats, and pause/resume compaction. There are no range scans, no ordered access and no write batches or transactions.
how_it_is_fast: It uses a Bitcask/Haystack-style log-structured hash design. Every write is a sequential append to a data file (1 GB in the examples). An in-memory hash index maps each key to its file id, value offset, size and sequence number, so a get needs at most one positional disk read (read amplification 1). The index lives off the Java heap to avoid GC pressure. It is derived from OHC, segmented like Java 7's ConcurrentHashMap with 2x-cores segments, and has an optional slab memory pool for fixed-size keys. A rate-limited background thread rewrites any file whose stale fraction passes a threshold, so a 50% threshold gives about 2x write amplification. Yahoo measured 10-12x for RocksDB on its own workload. Deletes go to separate tombstone files, and no key ordering is maintained.
when_to_use: JVM services doing only point lookups, where the data set is much larger than RAM but every key plus about 20 bytes of metadata fits in memory (e.g. 8-byte keys with 1-10 KB values)
Write-heavy random insert/update workloads on SSD where LSM write amplification is the bottleneck: 127 vs 10 MB/s fill-random and 19 vs 2 MB/s random update against RocksDB in the project's test
One writer thread (e.g. a consumer draining a Kafka log) with many concurrent readers that need sub-millisecond p99 reads, the setup Yahoo ran in production
Kyoto Cabinet replacement in Java where fast crash recovery matters: only the one or two files being written need repair
when_not_to_use: You need range scans, ordered or prefix iteration, write batches, transactions or column families. Stay on RocksDB.
Keys are longer than 127 bytes, or the whole key set will not fit in RAM. Yahoo quotes about 44 GB for 1 billion 8-byte keys with the memory pool and about 64 GB without.
Bulk loads in sorted key order: RocksDB won that test (165 vs 133 MB/s). Disk use is also higher (556 GB vs RocksDB's 504 GB after 500M random updates).
Restart time matters: opening a database scans every index and tombstone file to rebuild the index, which the README says can take minutes.

You need a maintained dependency on a current JDK: the code targets Java 8 and relies on sun.misc.Unsafe, which is deprecated in JDK 23 (issue #63). The last release was 2021, and the Yahoo artifacts are not on Maven Central.

integration.dependencies: slf4j-api 1.7.12, Guava 18.0, JNA 4.1.0 (native malloc for the off-heap index); lz4 1.3 optional. Jar is com.oath.halodb:halodb 0.5.6, published only to GitHub Packages (needs a token) or via JitPack as com.github.yahoo:HaloDB; not on Maven Central.
integration.min_toolchain: Java 8 (compiled with source/target 1.8; CI runs only JDK 8). The README says newer JDKs are untested. A user in issue #63 reports it running on Java 22.
integration.platforms: The README says it was tested on Linux x86 and macOS. It needs a 64-bit JVM (the Uns class rejects address sizes above 8 bytes). Windows has an open bug where repair after an unclean shutdown fails (issue #23). Tuning advice: disable Transparent Huge Pages and set vm.swappiness=0.
integration.thread_safety: get() is safe from many threads concurrently. put() and delete() share one global ReentrantLock, so writes are effectively single-threaded (issue #7; finer locking is a TODO). A LOCK file allows only one process per database directory.

gotchas: The key limit is really 127 bytes (Byte.MAX_VALUE, checked in HaloDBInternal.put), not the 128 the README says. With the memory pool on, any key longer than the declared fixedKeySize is rejected.

Writes are not durable by default. They land in the OS page cache and are synced only after flushDataSizeBytes accumulates, unless enableSyncWrites(true) is set, which the author says costs significant write throughput. After a power loss, interleaved puts and deletes keep only partial ordering.
Interrupting a thread during IO makes the JVM close the FileChannel it was using, and the README warns not to do this.

Set setNumberOfRecords (about 2x the expected key count) up front, or the off-heap index has to rehash. Without the memory pool every write calls native malloc, so the README recommends jemalloc against fragmentation.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick HaloDB when you must stay inside a Java process and only need point gets, puts and deletes. Badger and Pogreb (Go) and NuDB (C++) cannot be embedded directly in the JVM. If you can leave the JVM or need ordered access, one of those siblings or RocksDB fits better.
verified_claims_summary: This is a first-party benchmark from about 2018: 500M records with 8-byte keys and 1 KB values (about 500 GB) on 2x Xeon E5-2680, 128 GB RAM, one Samsung PM863 SSD and RHEL 6. It compared HaloDB with rocksdbjni 5.7.2 (WAL disabled, Snappy on L2 and above, custom 10 MB L1 tuning) and KyotoCabinet; the JVM version and flags are not stated. HaloDB won fill-random 127 vs 10 MB/s, random update 19 vs 2 MB/s, 32-thread random reads 94,409 vs 59,936 ops/s (about 1.6x) and mixed read+update 45,750 vs 8,625 reads/s and 6,144 vs 2,691 writes/s. It lost sorted-order fill to RocksDB, 133 vs 165 MB/s.
status_note: The Yahoo repository is abandoned: the last release is v0.5.6 (May 2021), the last commit is from April 2023, and an open 'Project status?' issue has no maintainer reply. It is Apache-2.0 and about 50 Java files, so it can be vendored. The live continuation is the community fork outr/HaloDB (halodb-revive 0.7.0 on Maven Central, JDK 22+, FFM instead of Unsafe, longer keys, prefix scans), but that fork is new and has almost no adoption.
